BACKGROUND: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO 2 Rec) is slow in advanced heart failure. We sought to establish easily derived VO 2 Rec measures and evaluate their cardiospecificity and prognostic relevance in patients with dyspnea on exertion. We further sought to determine VO 2 Rec modifiability proportional to changes in cardiac function with disease-specific treatment of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. METHODS: VO 2 Rec patterns were evaluated in relation to cardiac performance and the primary outcome of heart failure hospitalization or death in a referral cohort with dyspnea on exertion undergoing cardiopulmonary exercise testing with hemodynamic monitoring (MGH-ExS [Massachusetts General Hospital Exercise Study]). We then investigated longitudinal measures of VO 2 Rec in the pivotal phase 3 randomized controlled trial SEQUOIA-HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) of aficamten versus placebo for 24 weeks in participants with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. For both cohorts, VO 2 Rec was uniformly measured as time for VO 2 to decline by >0%, 12.5% (VO 2 T 12.5% ), 25%, and 50% of peak VO 2 . RESULTS: Among 814 MGH-ExS patients (58±16 years of age, 58% women), those with a longer VO 2 T 12.5% (≥35 versus <35 seconds) demonstrated elevated exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure to cardiac output slope ( P <0.0001) with no difference in peripheral oxygen extraction ( P =0.11). For each 15-second increase in VO 2 T 12.5% , the hazard ratio for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death was 1.54 (95% CI, 1.35–1.76; P <0.001). In SEQUOIA-HCM participants with cardiopulmonary exercise testing at baseline and week 24 (n=263, 59.1±2.9 years of age, 41% women), baseline VO 2 T 12.5% was 45±20 seconds and improved 8 seconds (95% CI, −12 to −5 seconds; P <0.001) with aficamten treatment compared with placebo at 24 weeks. Participants treated with aficamten versus placebo were more likely to improve VO 2 T 12.5% by ≥15 seconds (odds ratio [OR], 3.7 [95% CI, 1.9–6.9]; number needed to treat=4.8). Shortening of VO 2 T 12.5% correlated with reduced NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I, and left ventricular outflow tract gradient (all P <005). CONCLUSIONS: This study established VO 2 T 12.5% as a new measure that reflects cardiac performance during exercise and predicted heart failure event-free survival. Furthermore, VO 2 T 12.5% improved proportional to improvements in left ventricular outflow tract gradient and cardiac biomarkers in response to aficamten treatment, a cardiospecific therapy for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The simplicity and physiological relevance of VO 2 T 12.5% support its regular inclusion in cardiopulmonary exercise testing protocols evaluating cardiac function during exercise. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05186818. aficamten cardiac myosin cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic exercise test heart failure, diastolic post-exercise recovery OPEN-ACCESS TRUE SDC T Clinical Perspective What Is New? This study reports multiple novel measures of oxygen uptake (VO 2 ) recovery after incremental exercise, highlighting that early VO2 recovery, measured as the time to recover 12.5% of peak VO2 (VO2T12.5%), is an easily derived measurement of metabolic resilience that closely reflects cardiac but not peripheral performance during exercise and predicts heart failure outcomes. In a separate clinical trial cohort from the SEQUOIA--HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) trial, we demonstrated that VO2T12.5% improves proportionate to improvements in cardiac function in response to aficamten treatment, a myocardial disease–specific intervention in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. What Are the Clinical Implications? Measurements of VO 2 recovery are not currently reported in cardiopulmonary exercise tests conducted in clinical practice or in clinical trials. VO 2 recovery assessment is noninvasive, simple to perform, and holds promise in helping to ascertain cardiospecific limitations to exercise capacity. VO2T12.5% complements other physiological measurements assessed during exercise and merits incorporation into cardiopulmonary exercise testing–based assessments of cardiac performance. VO2T12.5% deserves consideration as an important clinical trial end point when evaluating future cardiac interventions.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO2Rec/VO2 T 12.5%) kinetics in various heart failure conditions (HFrEF, HFpEF, oHCM) and their response to cardiospecific treatments like aficamten.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO2Rec), particularly VO2 T 12.5%, provides a quantitative measure of metabolic resilience and directly reflects cardiac performance during exercise, not peripheral oxygen extraction. Prolonged VO2Rec and VO2 T 12.5% are linked to impaired central cardiac function due to slower cardiac output (CO) and stroke volume (SV) augmentation and recovery, leading to elevated left ventricular filling pressures and increased PCWP/CO slope. Diagnostic criteria for HFpEF-HDI are based on these hemodynamic impairments, often accompanied by elevated NT-proBNP or structural abnormalities. Aficamten, a cardiospecific therapy, directly targets myocyte contractility in oHCM, improving cardiac function (e.g., reducing LVOT gradient) which, in turn, proportionally shortens VO2 T 12.5% and reduces cardiac biomarkers like NT-proBNP and hs-cTnI. Differential recovery kinetics of VO2 component variables (CO, Ca-vO2, SV, HR) provide mechanistic insight into VO2 T 12.5%'s cardiospecificity, with Ca-vO2 recovering more rapidly than CO, and SV recovery being delayed in prolonged VO2 T 12.5%.
related_biomarkers: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure to Cardiac Output Slope (PCWP/CO slope)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Aficamten treatment, individualized to achieve optimal LVOT-G reduction and preserved LVEF, significantly improved VO2 T 12.5% by 8 seconds (95% CI, -12 to -5 seconds; P <0.001) over 24 weeks compared to placebo, with an odds ratio of 3.7 (95% CI, 1.9–6.9) for a ≥15-second improvement, suggesting a number needed to treat <5. A clear dose-response was observed where each 15-second increase in prolonged VO2 T 12.5% corresponded to a 50% increase in the risk for HF hospitalization or all-cause death (HR 1.54 [1.35–1.76], P <0.001). VO2 T 12.5% demonstrated superior diagnostic performance (AUC 0.72) compared to VO2 T 0% (AUC 0.63) for differentiating HFpEF-HDI from noncardiac dyspnea, and similar performance to VO2 T 25% and VO2 T 50% (both AUC=0.75), indicating that later time points beyond VO2 T 0% are more discriminative, but VO2 T 12.5% offers sufficient diagnostic certainty without needing longer measurement periods.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: VO2 T 12.5% demonstrates cardiospecificity, as it closely tracks with invasively derived exercise hemodynamic indices of heart failure and reflects cardiac rather than peripheral performance (no difference in peripheral oxygen extraction, P=0.11). It consistently outperforms other noninvasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) measurements (e.g., peak VO2 % predicted, VE/VCO2 nadir, VO2/work slope) in identifying impaired cardiac performance, particularly in HFpEF, and differentiating HFpEF-HDI from noncardiac dyspnea. Its prognostic value for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death is independent of demographics, medication use, and peak VO2. The improvement in VO2 T 12.5% with aficamten treatment correlates proportionally with improvements in cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP, troponin) and reduction in LVOT obstruction, further supporting its specificity to cardiac function. Specific thresholds (e.g., ≥35 seconds for prolonged VO2 T 12.5%) are crucial for its diagnostic and prognostic utility.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Heterogeneous cohorts of patients with dyspnea on exertion, including those with severe heart failure (HFrEF, HFpEF), symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM), and individuals at risk for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death. This includes participants in the MGH-ExS study (mean age 58±16 years, high cardiometabolic risk, low exercise capacity) and the SEQUOIA-HCM trial (symptomatic oHCM, mean age 59±13 years).
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Prolonged post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery, specifically VO2 T 12.5% (≥35 seconds), serves as a robust diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for impaired central cardiac function and metabolic resilience. It effectively identifies Heart Failure with preserved Ejection Fraction - Hemodynamic Impairment (HFpEF-HDI), distinguishes it from noncardiac dyspnea, and identifies patients at significantly increased risk of heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death. A predominant central cardiac limitation to exercise is linked to a 5-fold greater risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. VO2 T 12.5% provides additive prognostic value when combined with other established markers like peak VO2 or NT-proBNP. Furthermore, VO2 T 12.5% is modifiable; its improvement, as seen with aficamten treatment in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, indicates improved cardiac performance and reflects therapeutic efficacy.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: VO2 T 12.5% functions as a crucial prognostic indicator for heart failure events (hospitalization and all-cause death) and for risk stratification in patients with impaired peak VO2 or elevated NT-proBNP. It offers significant diagnostic utility for identifying impaired central cardiac performance, distinguishing Heart Failure with preserved Ejection Fraction - Hemodynamic Impairment (HFpEF-HDI) from noncardiac dyspnea. Its improvement indicates a therapeutic/protective benefit, serving as a marker for the efficacy of cardiac-augmenting interventions like aficamten in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: VO2 T 12.5% is an easily derived, noninvasive, and simple-to-perform measurement with high ascertainability (94% within 1 minute) and physiological relevance. It robustly captures early recovery kinetics and consistently outperforms other noninvasive CPET measurements in identifying impaired cardiac performance in HFpEF, closely tracking with invasively derived exercise hemodynamic indices of HF. It discriminates hemodynamic impairment better than VO2 T 0% and offers similar diagnostic certainty as VO2 T 25% and VO2 T 50%, but requires shorter measurement periods. Its prognostic value remains significant even after adjusting for demographics and other CPET measures (adjusted AUC=0.67, P <0.001). While promising, some limitations include the lack of complete NT-proBNP or echocardiography data for all patients in some cohorts, and the absence of functional imaging or invasive hemodynamic measurements during exercise in the SEQUOIA-HCM study.
recommended_alternatives: CPET gas exchange measures previously established for clinical use in evaluation of patients with HF (percent predicted peak VO2, VO2/work slope, and VE/VCO2 nadir)
other relevant clinical covariates commonly used in HF prognostication (NT-proBNP and percent predicted VO2)
Future studies on recovery patterns of Fick variables at additional proximal time points of recovery
Direct comparison of VO2 T 12.5% to assessments of cardiac performance during exercise in oHCM in future studies
Further studies to compare readily derivable noninvasive VO2 Rec variables across broad patient populations.
